function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

Once you have the files ready, you can run the corresponding Git commands locally to commit and push them. Below is a step‑by‑step plan you can follow: | Step | What to do | Why | |------|------------|-----| | **1** | `git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git` | Pull the repo to your local machine. | | **2** | **Analyse** the repo’s structure (look at `package.json`, `src/`, `public/`, etc.). | Understand what the app needs (runtime, ports, env vars). | | | **2.1** Create a Dockerfile in the repo root. | Package the Node.js app into a container. | | | **2.2** Create Kubernetes YAML files (`deployment.yaml`, `service.yaml`) in a `k8s/` folder. | Deploy the container to a cluster. | | | **2.3** Create a GitHub Actions workflow (`.github/workflows/build.yml`). | Automate CI/CD on pushes to `main`. | | **3** | `git add .` | Stage all new/changed files. | | **4** | `git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, K8s manifests, and GitHub Actions workflow"`
`git push origin main` | Commit and push the changes. | --- ## 1. Clone the Repository ```bash git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git cd nodejs-welcome ``` --- ## 2. Analyse the Repo Open the repo locally and inspect: - `package.json` – lists dependencies, scripts, and the entry point (`main` field). - `src/` or `app/` – contains the server code. - Any `.env` or config files. - Look for a `PORT` environment variable or hard‑coded port. Assume the app listens on port `3000` (common for Node.js). --- ## 2.1 Dockerfile Create a file named `Dockerfile` in the repo root with the following content: ```dockerfile # Use official Node.js LTS image FROM node:20-alpine # Set working directory WORKDIR /usr/src/app # Copy package files first to leverage Docker cache COPY package*.json ./ # Install dependencies RUN npm ci --only=production # Copy the rest of the application COPY . . # Expose the port the app listens on EXPOSE 3000 # Start the application CMD ["npm", "start"] ``` *Why?* - `node:20-alpine` is lightweight and includes Node.js. - `npm ci` installs only production dependencies. - `EXPOSE 3000` tells Docker which port the container will listen on. - `CMD ["npm", "start"]` runs the script defined in `package.json`. --- ## 2.2 Kubernetes YAMLs Create a folder `k8s/` and add two files: ### `k8s/deployment.yaml` ```yaml apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: nodejs-welcome spec: replicas: 3 selector: matchLabels: app: nodejs-welcome template: metadata: labels: app: nodejs-welcome spec: containers: - name: nodejs-welcome image: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest # Update with your registry/tag ports: - containerPort: 3000 env: - name: NODE_ENV value: production resources: limits: cpu: "500m" memory: "512Mi" requests: cpu: "250m" memory: "256Mi" ``` ### `k8s/service.yaml` ```yaml apiVersion: v1 kind: Service metadata: name: nodejs-welcome spec: type: LoadBalancer selector: app: nodejs-welcome ports: - protocol: TCP port: 80 targetPort: 3000 ``` *Why?* - Deployment creates 3 replicas for high availability. - Service exposes the app on port `80` externally, mapping to container port `3000`. - `LoadBalancer` lets you expose the app via an external IP (works on cloud providers). --- ## 2.3 GitHub Actions Workflow Create a folder `.github/workflows/` and add `build.yml`: ```yaml name: Build and Push Docker Image on: push: branches: - main jobs: build: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Checkout repository uses: actions/checkout@v4 - name: Set up Docker Buildx uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3 - name: Log in to GitHub Container Registry uses: docker/login-action@v3 with: registry: ghcr.io username: ${{ github.actor }} password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }} - name: Build and push Docker image uses: docker/build-push-action@v5 with: context: . push: true tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest ``` *Why?* - Triggers on pushes to `main`. - Builds the Docker image from the repo root. - Pushes it to GitHub Container Registry (`ghcr.io`). - Uses the built‑in `GITHUB_TOKEN` for authentication. --- ## 3. Add All Changed Files ```bash git add . ``` --- ## 4. Commit & Push ```bash git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, K8s manifests, and GitHub Actions workflow" git push origin main ``` --- ### Quick Checklist - [ ] Dockerfile exists in repo root. - [ ] `k8s/deployment.yaml` and `k8s/service.yaml` exist. - [ ] `.github/workflows/build.yml` exists. - [ ] All files are staged (`git status` shows them as added). - [ ] Commit message is descriptive. - [ ] Push succeeded (`git push` shows “Everything up‑to‑date” or similar). Once pushed, GitHub Actions will automatically run the workflow, build the image, and push it to GHCR. You can then deploy the app to Kubernetes using `kubectl apply -f k8s/`. Let me know if you need help with any of the individual steps!
